title: Exceptions as Signals
blurb: Stop checking before you leap: let failure raise, catch it at the boundary, and turn errors into data.

cells.title: EAFP: easier to ask forgiveness than permission
cells.body:
There are two ways to use a value that might be invalid. LBYL ('look before you leap') pre-checks: if key in d: ..., if s.isdigit(): .... EAFP just tries the operation and handles the exception if it fails. Python culture leans EAFP, and not just for brevity: the check and the operation can disagree (a key can be present but the value wrong; isdigit accepts digits that still fail to parse), and in concurrent code the world can change between check and use.

The reasoning payoff: with EAFP, the operation itself is the authority on what is valid. Your code has one source of truth instead of two parallel ones that drift apart. The try block should be as small as possible — wrap the one risky line, not the whole function — so the except clause can't accidentally swallow unrelated failures.

cells.title: Raising is designing a signal
cells.body:
Catching exceptions is only half the protocol — your own code should raise when it cannot honor its contract, and the exception type you choose is part of your API. ValueError says 'the caller gave me a bad value'; KeyError says 'that name is missing'; TypeError says 'wrong shape of input'. Callers write except ValueError against that promise, so raising the wrong category breaks code you have never seen.

When a domain needs its own vocabulary, subclass Exception: a custom class is catchable by name, carries a message, and can hold structured data as attributes. A raise is not a crash — it is a non-local return that says 'this path failed; someone upstream decide what to do'. Designing failure paths deliberately is what separates libraries people enjoy from libraries people tolerate.

cells.title: Recovery loops: skip, classify, retry
cells.body:
Real data pipelines meet three recovery shapes. Skip: one bad record must not kill the batch — wrap the risky parse in try/except and continue past failures, keeping a count so silence never hides a systemic problem. Classify: catch, inspect, and route the failure (log it, tag the row, bucket it by type). Retry: some failures are transient — a sensor or a network blip — so try again, but a bounded number of times, with a growing pause between attempts (exponential backoff), because hammering a struggling resource makes things worse.

Every shape shares one discipline: the loop must be able to end. Bounded retries, a maximum of one skip per record, a clear 'give up' path — unhandled failure inside a recovery loop is how jobs spin forever at 3 a.m. Write the exit conditions before the body.

exercise.title: Safe Gauge Reading
exercise.statement:
Fuel gauges on a fleet of trucks report their readings as strings over a noisy bus: "42", "-7", but also garbled fragments like "3.5", "12a" or the empty string. The dashboard needs a number or, when the transmission is unusable, a fallback value.

Implement safe_reading(text, fallback): the integer value of text when it parses as an integer literal, otherwise fallback. Solve it the EAFP way — attempt the conversion and handle the failure — rather than pre-validating the string character by character; Python's own parser is the authority on what an integer literal is.
constraints: text is always a string of at most 20 characters
int() accepts surrounding spaces and a leading + or - (so ' 15 ' is 15 and '+9' is 9)
strings like '3.5', '12a' and '' are NOT integer literals
hints: Who is the authority on what counts as an integer literal — your own character checks, or int() itself?
Attempt int(text) inside a try, and catch ValueError to return the fallback. One risky line, one handler, no pre-checks.
try: return int(text) except ValueError: return fallback. That's the whole function — everything else the tests probe comes free from int's own rules.
exercise.reasoning: The EAFP version delegates the definition of 'valid integer literal' to the one component that actually owns it: the int() constructor. Any pre-validation you write is a second, weaker copy of that definition — and it will disagree at the edges (surrounding spaces, a leading +, -0). Notice also what the except clause does NOT do: it catches ValueError specifically, so a TypeError from a genuinely wrong kind of input would still surface loudly. Narrow handlers are a feature — a bare except here would hide bugs in your own code, not just noisy data.

exercise.title: First Failure Per Component
exercise.statement:
A service writes log lines of the form LEVEL COMPONENT MESSAGE, where LEVEL is one of INFO, WARN or ERROR, COMPONENT is a single token, and MESSAGE is the rest of the line (it may contain spaces). The log is dirty: lines are truncated, levels are mistyped, junk gets interleaved. Your tool must skip any line that does not have three parts or whose level is not recognized, and never crash on the junk.

Implement first_errors(lines): a dict mapping each component to the MESSAGE of its first ERROR line. INFO and WARN lines are valid but contribute nothing. Skip malformed lines the EAFP way — attempt the three-way unpacking and let a ValueError mark the bad ones.
constraints: fields are separated by one or more spaces
components are single tokens; only the first ERROR per component is remembered

examples.call: first_errors(["ERROR DB pool exhausted", "INFO DB all good", "ERROR DB disk full"])
examples.why: the later DB error is ignored — only the first counts

examples.call: first_errors(["ERROR DB pool exhausted", "WARN NET flaky", "ERROR NET timeout"])
examples.why: each component contributes its first error

hints: How does line.split(None, 2) behave on a line with only two fields — and what exception does the three-way unpacking level, component, message = ... raise then?
Wrap the split-and-unpack in try/except ValueError and continue past bad lines. Then validate the level against the known set, and only ERROR lines with an unseen component get stored.
for line in lines: try to unpack line.split(None, 2) into three names (except ValueError: continue); skip unknown levels; if level == 'ERROR' and component not in firsts: firsts[component] = message.
exercise.reasoning: Two EAFP decisions do the work. First, tuple unpacking is the shape check: a, b, c = parts raises ValueError exactly when the line does not have three fields, so the malformed-line rule costs one except clause instead of a manual len() inspection — and it cannot drift out of sync with the real requirement. Second, the 'first error only' rule is a dict-membership question: store a component's message only when the key is absent, and later errors are ignored without counters or flags. Note how split(None, 2) caps the split so the MESSAGE part keeps its internal spaces — parsing limits are part of the contract, not an afterthought.

exercise.title: Retry With Backoff
exercise.statement:
A field sensor is flaky: sometimes it answers with a reading, sometimes it times out. You will simulate it deterministically. Write fetch_with_retry(plan, max_attempts) where plan[i] describes attempt i + 1: an int means the sensor returns that reading; the string "fail" means it times out.

The required structure is the whole exercise: define a custom exception SensorTimeout(Exception); write a helper that raises SensorTimeout when the plan says "fail" and returns the reading otherwise; and drive a retry loop that catches the exception and decides whether to try again. After the k-th failed attempt that is followed by another attempt, the client waits 2**(k-1) seconds (so the pauses grow 1, 2, 4, ...). Return a dict {"status": "ok" | "failed", "reading": int-or-None, "attempts": attempts actually made, "waited": total simulated pause}.
constraints: plan entries are ints or the exact string 'fail'
readings may be negative — temperature sensors go below zero
no time or sleep module: waiting is simulated arithmetic only

examples.why: the first attempt succeeds, so no retries and no pause
one timeout costs a 1-second pause, then the second attempt succeeds

exercise.starter:
class SensorTimeout(Exception):
    """The sensor did not answer within its window."""


def fetch_with_retry(plan, max_attempts):
    """Simulate up to max_attempts sensor reads from the plan.

    plan[i] is the reading for attempt i+1, or "fail" for a timeout
    (the helper must RAISE SensorTimeout in that case, and this loop
    must CATCH it). Waits 2**(k-1) seconds after failed attempt k
    whenever another attempt follows. Returns the outcome dict.
    """
    pass

tests.label: success on the last allowed try
budget spent before plan runs out

hints: Who should know that attempt i failed — the caller checking a return code, or a helper that raises and a loop that catches? Which one keeps the retry loop readable?

attempt(i) raises SensorTimeout on 'fail' and returns the reading otherwise. The loop calls it in a try; on success return the ok dict immediately; on timeout, add the pause (1, 2, 4, ...) only if another attempt is coming.

waited = 0; for i in range(max_attempts): try: reading = attempt(i); return ok-dict — except SensorTimeout: if i + 1 < max_attempts: waited += 2 ** i. After the loop, return the failed dict with attempts = max_attempts.
exercise.reasoning: The custom exception turns a messy return-code protocol into clean separation: the helper's only job is to signal (raise), and the loop's only job is to decide (catch and retry). The two bookkeeping invariants are where correctness lives. First, attempts counts tries actually made, so it is i + 1 on success and max_attempts on exhaustion — never a counter you increment in two places. Second, the pause after failure k is charged only when a retry follows: waiting after your final failure wastes a second nobody uses, which is why the all-fail case with 3 attempts waits 1 + 2 = 3 seconds, not 7. Getting both right is exactly the discipline real retry policies (and their unit tests) demand.
